name: Megapixels
description: Computes an image sensor's resolution in megapixels as width times height in pixels, divided by one million. It gives the total pixel count in millions.
notes: Width and height are in pixels; the result is the total, not a linear dimension. Effective (recorded) megapixels can be slightly below the sensor's nominal count.

name: Aspect ratio
description: Computes the aspect ratio of an image or screen as its width divided by its height. A value of about 1.778 corresponds to the common 16:9 widescreen format.
notes: Width and height must use the same unit so the ratio is dimensionless. The result is a decimal ratio; convert to a form like 16:9 separately if needed.

name: Pixel density (DPI)
description: Computes a display's pixel density in dots per inch as the diagonal pixel count (hypotenuse of width and height) divided by the diagonal size in inches. Higher DPI means a sharper, finer image.
notes: Width and height are in pixels and diagonal in inches; hypot gives the diagonal pixel length. Higher DPI on a screen means finer detail, unlike loosely used print DPI.

name: Total Pixels
description: Counts the total number of pixels in an image or display by multiplying its width by its height in pixels. For example 1920 by 1080 gives about 2.07 million pixels.
notes: This counts pixel positions, not memory; storage also depends on bits per pixel. Divide by one million for megapixels.

name: Pixels Per Inch (PPI)
description: Computes a display's pixel density by dividing the diagonal resolution in pixels, found from the Pythagorean combination of width and height pixels, by the physical diagonal size in inches.
notes: The diagonal size must be in inches; higher PPI means finer detail. It assumes square pixels and a screen whose pixel aspect ratio matches its physical shape.

name: Dot Pitch
description: Gives the spacing between adjacent pixel centers in millimeters by dividing 25.4, the number of millimeters in an inch, by the pixel density in pixels per inch. Higher density gives a smaller dot pitch.
notes: The constant 25.4 fixes the unit to millimeters per pixel. Dot pitch is the inverse of PPI, so denser displays have finer pitch.

name: Representable Colors
description: Gives the total number of distinct colors that can be represented at a given color depth, as 2 raised to the number of bits. A 24-bit depth yields about 16.7 million colors.
notes: For per-channel RGB the total bits are the sum across channels, so 8 bits each gives 24-bit color. An alpha channel adds transparency levels, not colors.

name: RGB Relative Luminance
description: Estimates the perceived brightness of an RGB color as a weighted sum of its red, green, and blue channels, using coefficients 0.2126, 0.7152, and 0.0722. Green contributes most to perceived luminance.
notes: These Rec. 709 weights assume linear (gamma-decoded) channel values; applying them to raw sRGB values gives only an approximation. Result scales with the channel range used.

name: Contrast Ratio
description: Gives a display's contrast ratio as the maximum luminance divided by the minimum luminance. A result of 500 is written as 500:1 and indicates how distinct the brightest and darkest tones are.
notes: Both luminances must use the same unit, and the minimum must be greater than zero. Measurement conditions strongly affect the value, so quoted ratios vary widely.

name: 3D Euclidean Distance
description: Computes the straight-line Euclidean distance between two points in 3D space as the square root of the summed squared differences of their x, y, and z coordinates. It gives the shortest distance separating the points.
notes: All coordinates must share the same units, which the result inherits. Using hypot avoids intermediate overflow or underflow when coordinate differences are very large or very small.

name: Unit Vector X-Component
description: Computes the x-component of the unit vector obtained by normalizing a 3D vector, dividing its x component by the vector's length. The result is the direction cosine of the vector with respect to the x-axis.
notes: The vector must be nonzero or the length is zero and the division is undefined. The output lies in [-1,1] and equals the cosine of the angle between the vector and the x-axis.

name: Angle Between Vectors (3D)
description: Computes the angle in radians between two 3D vectors by taking the arccosine of their dot product divided by the product of their magnitudes. It quantifies how much the two directions diverge.
notes: Both vectors must be nonzero. Floating-point rounding can push the ratio slightly outside [-1,1], so it is often clamped before acos; the result ranges from 0 to pi.

name: Inverse Linear Interpolation
description: Computes inverse linear interpolation, returning the fraction t in [0,1] that value v occupies between endpoints a and b. It answers where a value falls on a range as a normalized parameter.
notes: Requires a not equal to b. Values of v outside [a,b] return results outside [0,1], and it is the inverse of the standard lerp a+t*(b-a).

name: Gamma Correction (Encoding)
description: Applies gamma encoding to a linear color value by raising it to the power 1/g, compressing linear light into a perceptually encoded signal for storage or display. Higher gamma darkens mid-tones more before encoding inversion.
notes: Input c should be a normalized value in [0,1]; the same range is preserved on output. This is a pure power law and does not include the linear toe used by the full sRGB curve.

name: sRGB to Linear (Gamma 2.4)
description: Converts an sRGB color value to linear space using the standard curve's power segment, ((c+0.055)/1.055) raised to 2.4. This linearizes gamma-encoded colors so lighting and filtering can be computed physically correctly.
notes: This applies only to the upper segment; the exact sRGB spec uses a linear formula c/12.92 for c at or below about 0.04045. Input c should be normalized to [0,1].

name: CIE Lightness (L*)
description: Computes CIE L*, the perceptual lightness of a color, as 116 times the cube root of its relative luminance minus 16. It maps luminance onto a roughly uniform scale from 0 (black) to 100 (white).
notes: Relative luminance y should be normalized so that the reference white gives y=1 and thus L*=100. This uses only the cube-root branch; the CIE formula switches to a linear branch for very small y.

name: Vertical Field of View
description: Computes the vertical field of view of a camera from its horizontal field of view and aspect ratio, as 2 times the arctangent of tan(hfov/2) divided by the aspect ratio. It gives the angular extent seen vertically.
notes: Both the input and output angles are in radians, and the aspect ratio is width divided by height. For a wide aspect ratio the vertical FOV is smaller than the horizontal one.

name: View Frustum Height
description: Computes the height of a camera view frustum at a given distance from the camera, as 2 times the distance times the tangent of half the vertical field of view. It tells how tall the visible region is at that plane.
notes: The FOV must be in radians and stay below pi so the tangent is positive and finite. The output height shares the distance's units, and width follows by multiplying by the aspect ratio.

name: Focal Length from FOV
description: Computes the lens focal length that produces a given field of view for a sensor of a given size, as half the sensor size divided by the tangent of half the field of view. Wider fields of view require shorter focal lengths.
notes: Sensor size and focal length share units (here mm), and the FOV must be in radians and below pi. Use the sensor dimension matching the FOV direction: width for horizontal, height for vertical.

name: Frame Time from FPS
description: Computes the time budget available per frame in milliseconds by dividing 1000 by the frame rate in frames per second. It shows how long each frame may take to sustain a target frame rate.
notes: FPS must be positive; 60 fps yields about 16.67 ms per frame and 30 fps about 33.33 ms. Any frame exceeding this budget causes stutter or a dropped frame.

name: Rec. 709 Luma
description: Computes luma using the Rec. 709 (HDTV) coefficients, a weighted sum of the red, green, and blue channels reflecting the eye's greater sensitivity to green. It condenses a color into a single brightness value.
notes: Strictly this weights gamma-encoded R'G'B' to give luma (Y'), not linear luminance. Inputs are normalized channel values in [0,1]; the fixed weights sum to 1.

name: Rec. 2020 Luma
description: Computes luma using the Rec. 2020 (UHDTV) coefficients, a weighted sum of red, green, and blue tuned for the wider color gamut of ultra-high-definition video. Green is weighted most and blue least.
notes: These coefficients differ from Rec. 709 because the primaries differ; the weights still sum to 1. Inputs are normalized channels in [0,1], and this gives gamma-domain luma rather than linear luminance.

name: Total Pixel Count
description: Computes the total number of pixels in an image or display by multiplying its width in pixels by its height in pixels. This gives the resolution as a single pixel count, such as roughly 2.07 million for 1920 by 1080.
notes: Both dimensions are in pixels and should be positive integers. This counts pixels only and does not account for color depth or bytes per pixel in memory.

name: Diagonal PPI
description: Computes a display's pixel density in pixels per inch by dividing the diagonal pixel count (hypotenuse of width and height in pixels) by the physical diagonal size in inches. Higher PPI means a sharper, finer image.
notes: Width and height are in pixels while the diagonal is in inches, and the result is ppi. It assumes square pixels and a diagonal that matches the pixel aspect ratio.

name: Icosphere Triangle Count
description: Computes the number of triangular faces in an icosphere after n subdivision levels, as 20 times 4 to the power n. Each subdivision splits every triangle into four, starting from the icosahedron's 20 faces.
notes: The subdivision level n should be a non-negative integer, giving 20 faces at n=0. Triangle count grows exponentially, so high subdivision levels quickly produce very large meshes.

name: Normalized Device Depth
description: Computes the nonlinear normalized device depth stored in a perspective depth buffer for a point at view-space depth z, given the near and far plane distances. It maps the depth range into [0,1] with fine precision near the camera.
notes: Requires z, n, and f positive with f greater than n. The mapping is nonlinear, concentrating precision near the near plane, which causes z-fighting for distant surfaces.

name: Linearize Depth Buffer
description: Recovers the linear view-space depth from a normalized depth-buffer value zn in [0,1], given the near and far plane distances. It inverts the perspective depth mapping to return an actual distance from the camera.
notes: This assumes zn is in the [0,1] convention, so it is remapped to NDC via 2*zn-1. Requires f greater than n, and the result is in the same units as the plane distances.

name: Texel Density (Texels per Unit)
description: Computes texel density as the texture resolution in pixels divided by the world-space size it covers, giving texels per world unit. It indicates how finely a texture is applied to a surface.
notes: World size must be nonzero and share consistent units, giving px per unit. Matching texel density across assets keeps surface detail visually uniform throughout a scene.

name: Mipmap Chain Length
description: Computes the number of mipmap levels in a full chain for a texture, as the floor of the base-2 logarithm of the larger dimension plus one. The chain runs from the full-resolution image down to a single texel.
notes: Width and height are in pixels; the larger side determines the count. This gives a full chain down to 1x1, so a 1024-wide texture yields 11 levels including the base.

name: Schlick's Fresnel Approximation
description: Computes Schlick's approximation of the Fresnel reflectance, interpolating from the base reflectance f0 at normal incidence up toward 1 at grazing angles using (1-cos theta) to the fifth power. It models how reflectivity rises at shallow viewing angles.
notes: Here c is the cosine of the angle between the view and the surface normal, in [0,1]. f0 is the reflectance at head-on incidence; the result approaches 1 as c approaches 0 (grazing).

name: Light Attenuation (Quadratic)
description: Computes how much a point light dims with distance using constant, linear, and quadratic falloff terms. The result is a multiplier between 0 and 1 applied to the light intensity, where larger distances give a smaller factor.
notes: The three coefficients are tunable and dimensionless; there is no single physically correct set. Pure inverse-square light uses only kq, so the constant term mainly prevents the value from exceeding 1 at short range.

name: Quadratic Bézier (1D)
description: Evaluates a quadratic Bézier curve at parameter t using three control values P0, P1, and P2. The result is a smooth blend that starts at P0 when t is 0 and ends at P2 when t is 1, bending toward the middle control point P1.
notes: The parameter t should lie in 0 to 1; values outside this range extrapolate the curve. The curve generally does not pass through P1, which only pulls the path toward itself.

name: Cubic Bézier (1D)
description: Evaluates a cubic Bézier curve at parameter t from four control values P0 through P3. The result starts at P0 at t equal to 0 and ends at P3 at t equal to 1, with P1 and P2 shaping the curvature in between.
notes: The parameter t should stay in 0 to 1; outside it the curve extrapolates. The curve touches only the endpoints P0 and P3, while the interior points P1 and P2 are not generally reached.

name: Smoothstep Interpolation
description: Applies the smoothstep function 3t²−2t³ to a normalized input t. It maps 0 to 0 and 1 to 1 with an S-shaped curve whose slope is zero at both ends, giving smooth ease-in and ease-out transitions.
notes: Input t is expected in 0 to 1; clamp it first because outside that range the polynomial overshoots. This gives continuous first derivatives but not second, so use smootherstep if smoother acceleration is needed.

name: Bilinear Interpolation
description: Interpolates a value inside a unit square from its four corner values using fractional coordinates u and v. Each corner is weighted by how close u and v are to it, blending the four corners into one smoothly varying result.
notes: The weights u and v should each lie in 0 to 1 measuring position within the cell. The result is exact at the four corners but the interpolation is not truly linear along diagonals.

name: Solid Angle of Cone
description: Computes the solid angle in steradians subtended by a right circular cone with the given half-angle at its apex. It ranges from 0 for a needle-thin cone up to 4π when the half-angle reaches π, covering the full sphere.
notes: The half-angle must be in radians, not degrees, and measures from the cone axis to its edge. A hemisphere corresponds to a half-angle of π/2, giving 2π steradians.

name: Texture Memory Footprint
description: Calculates the storage size in bytes of an uncompressed texture from its width, height, and bits per pixel. It multiplies the pixel count by the bit depth and divides by 8 to convert bits to bytes.
notes: This ignores mipmaps, which add roughly one third more, and any block-based compression such as DXT or ASTC. Add per-mip levels separately if the texture is mipmapped.

name: Reinhard Tone Mapping Operator
description: Maps a high-dynamic-range luminance value to a displayable range using the Reinhard operator L/(1+L). Any nonnegative input is compressed into the interval 0 to 1, with large values approaching but never reaching 1.
notes: This is the simplest global Reinhard form and tends to desaturate bright highlights. Luminance should be nonnegative; extended variants add a white point to let very bright pixels clip to pure white.

name: HSV Chroma
description: Computes chroma, the colorfulness of an RGB color, as the difference between its largest and smallest channel values. A result of 0 means a gray, while a larger value means a more vivid, saturated hue.
notes: Inputs are typically normalized to 0 to 1, so chroma also lands in that range. Chroma is not the same as HSV saturation, which divides this difference by the maximum channel.

name: WCAG Contrast Ratio
description: Computes the WCAG contrast ratio between two relative luminances by adding 0.05 to each and dividing the lighter by the darker. The result ranges from 1 for identical colors up to 21 for black against white.
notes: The first input must be the lighter luminance and the second the darker, or the ratio comes out below 1. WCAG AA normally requires at least 4.5 for normal text and 3 for large text.

name: Sphere Signed Distance Function
description: Returns the signed distance from a point (x,y,z) to the surface of a sphere of the given radius centered at the origin. It is negative inside the sphere, zero on the surface, and positive outside, equal to the point distance minus the radius.
notes: The point coordinates and radius must share the same length unit. This SDF assumes a sphere centered at the origin; shift the coordinates first for an off-center sphere.

name: Blinn-Phong Specular Reflection
description: Computes the specular reflection intensity in the Blinn-Phong lighting model as the specular coefficient ks times the dot product of the surface normal and half-vector (N·H), raised to the shininess exponent.
notes: NdotH is given directly here in the range -1 to 1 since the expression engine has no built-in 3D vector/dot-product support; it should be clamped to 0 before raising to a power in a real renderer to avoid undefined results for facing-away surfaces. Higher shininess produces a smaller, tighter highlight.
